title: How to Detect Hidden Cameras in Hotel Rooms
excerpt: Reflection, infrared, and radio each catch different hidden cameras. How the three methods work, where each fails, and the tells no tool replaces.
body:
No single gadget finds every hidden camera. The honest approach stacks three detection methods — reflection, infrared, and radio — because each one catches what the other two miss. Here is how each method works, what it cannot do, and the physical tells that no tool replaces.

Method one: the reflection sweep

A camera lens is a curved piece of glass, and curved glass returns a bright glint when light hits it at an angle. Kill the lights, hold a flashlight at hip height, and sweep slowly across surfaces, watching for a dot that glints while the surrounding material stays dark. Move the light, not your eyes: a fixed beam hides the glint in its own glare.

The fingernail test on mirrors

Touch your fingernail to any large mirror. If your nail touches its reflection with no gap, the mirror is likely glass on solid backing; a visible gap can indicate a two-way mirror. It is an imperfect screen, not proof, so a suspicious mirror earns the same response as a suspicious hole.

Method two: infrared with a phone camera

Many hidden cameras use infrared LEDs for night vision, and some phone cameras can see that infrared light as a purple or white dot glowing in a dark room. Whether yours can depends on the infrared filter in your specific phone, so calibrate first: in a dark room, point a TV remote at your phone and press buttons while watching the screen. If the remote's LED glows, your phone sees infrared; if not, skip this method entirely.

Why the infrared check is inconsistent

Phone manufacturers fit different infrared-blocking filters over their cameras, and many detector apps only flash the screen while claiming to scan. A phone that shows nothing may simply have a good filter, not a clean room.

Method three: RF and network detection

RF detectors listen for the radio signals a camera emits while streaming live. They catch transmitting cameras and nothing else — a camera recording to an internal card emits nothing, ever. Network-scanning apps list devices on the hotel WiFi, but only if the camera joined that same network, which many never do. Both tools have real uses and real blind spots; our detector app investigation and phone detection walkthrough go deeper on each.

The physical tells no gadget replaces

  • Out-of-place newness: a crisp object among worn decor, or a decor item still factory-sealed.
  • Unexplained holes: a dark dot on a speaker, a vent grille with extra openings.
  • Aiming at beds or bathrooms: an object positioned to watch where people undress.
  • Doubled hardware: two alarm clocks, a second smoke detector, a phone charger with no phone.

Where to sweep first

Work the highest-value spots in order: smoke detector, wall vents, outlets and power strips, the television and its surround, then decor near the bed and anything near the bathroom entrance. These are the spots that combine height, concealment, and a clear line of sight — the three things a hidden camera needs to be useful to whoever placed it.

The cameras no sweep can find

Every method above has a blind spot, and honest coverage admits it. A camera recording to an internal memory card emits no radio signal, joins no network, and shows no infrared if its night vision is off or absent. In daylight it is optically silent too, visible only as a physical lens. A device wired into mains power never blinks a low-battery warning and never needs retrieving, so it can sit indefinitely. No phone app detects any of these; only the physical inspection, the holes, glints, and wrong placements, has a chance.

That is why the order of operations matters: tools first for speed, eyes last for certainty, never the reverse. A sweep that finds nothing has reduced the risk, not removed it, so weigh what you do in the room accordingly and keep sensitive conversations and valuables out of sightlines you could not fully clear. The goal is a room you have actually examined, not a certificate of cleanliness no method can honestly issue.

If a sweep turns up a device

Do not touch it; your fingerprints obscure evidence and may alert whoever is watching. Photograph it from the doorway, leave the room, and call the police, then notify the front desk from a safe place. Laws on hidden cameras vary by state, and recording in a private space without consent is illegal in most US states, but penalties and definitions differ, so check your own jurisdiction — our state-by-state guide is a starting point. Document the room number, the date, and the exact time you found the device; that timeline is what investigators will ask for first.
